claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 destabilizes kinetochore-microtubule (k-MT) attachments to promote faithful chromosome segregation.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that Cyclin A/Cdk1 destabilizes k-MT attachments to promote faithful chromosome segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: 156 Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrates were identified in prometaphase using quantitative phosphoproteomics.
source: Here, we use quantitative phosphoproteomics to identify 156 Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrates in prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MYPT1 is a Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrate.
source: One Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrate is myosin phosphatase targeting subunit 1 (MYPT1), and we show that MYPT1 localization to kinetochores depends on Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity and that MYPT1 destabilizes k-MT attachments by negatively regulating Plk1 at kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation and localization changes.

claim: MYPT1 localization to kinetochores depends on Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity.
source: One Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrate is myosin phosphatase targeting subunit 1 (MYPT1), and we show that MYPT1 localization to kinetochores depends on Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity and that MYPT1 destabilizes k-MT attachments by negatively regulating Plk1 at kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing MYPT1 localization changes upon Cyclin A depletion.

claim: MYPT1 destabilizes k-MT attachments by negatively regulating Plk1 at kinetochores.
source: One Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrate is myosin phosphatase targeting subunit 1 (MYPT1), and we show that MYPT1 localization to kinetochores depends on Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity and that MYPT1 destabilizes k-MT attachments by negatively regulating Plk1 at kinetochores.
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation experiments showing changes in k-MT stability upon MYPT1 depletion.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 phosphorylation primes MYPT1 for Plk1 binding.
source: Thus, Cyclin A/Cdk1 phosphorylation primes MYPT1 for Plk1 binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing phosphorylation at Ser473 and previous literature on priming phosphorylation.

claim: Priming of PBIP1 by Plk1 itself (self-priming) increased in MYPT1-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, priming of PBIP1 by Plk1 itself (self-priming) increased in MYPT1-depleted cells showing that MYPT1 provides a molecular link between the processes of Cdk1-dependent priming and self-priming of Plk1 substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data showing increased pPBIP1 Thr78 in MYPT1-depleted cells.

claim: MYPT1 provides a molecular link between Cdk1-dependent priming and self-priming of Plk1 substrates.
source: Interestingly, priming of PBIP1 by Plk1 itself (self-priming) increased in MYPT1-depleted cells showing that MYPT1 provides a molecular link between the processes of Cdk1-dependent priming and self-priming of Plk1 substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing coordinated changes in PBIP1 phosphorylation and Plk1 activity.

claim: Cross-regulation exists between Cyclin A/Cdk1-dependent and Plk1-dependent phosphorylation of substrates during mitosis.
source: These data demonstrate cross-regulation between Cyclin A/Cdk1-dependent and Plk1-dependent phosphorylation of substrates during mitosis to ensure efficient correction of k-MT attachment errors necessary for high mitotic fidelity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and functional experiments showing interconnected regulation.

claim: Hyperstable k-MTs are an underlying cause of elevated chromosome mis-segregation in aneuploid tumor cells.
source: Indeed, hyperstable k-MTs are an underlying cause of the elevated frequency of chromosome mis-segregation associated with chromosomal instability (CIN) observed in a majority of aneuploid tumor cells (Thompson et al., 2010; Cimini and Degrassi, 2005; Cimini, 2008; Weaver and Cleveland, 2007; Bakhoum et al., 2009a; Bakhoum et al., 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Systematically destabilizing k-MT attachments restores faithful chromosome segregation to tumor cells with high chromosome mis-segregation rates.
source: Systematically destabilizing k-MT attachments was shown to be sufficient to restore faithful chromosome segregation to tumor cells that otherwise exhibited exceptionally high chromosome mis-segregation rates (Bakhoum et al., 2009b; Kabeche and Compton, 2013; Stolz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: There is a causal relationship between k-MT attachment stability and the propensity for chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Thus, there is a causal relationship between the stability of k-MT attachments and the propensity for chromosome mis-segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from cited literature and experimental data.

claim: Plk1 is an essential mitotic kinase that regulates many aspects of mitosis.
source: For example, Polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1) is an essential mitotic kinase that regulates many aspects of mitosis (extensively reviewed in [Schmucker and Sumara, 2014; Petronczki et al., 2008; van Vugt and Medema, 2005]), including the stabilization of k-MT attachments in prometaphase (Lénárt et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Moutinho-Santos et al., 2012; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Hood et al., 2012; Maia et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to review articles and primary literature.

claim: Plk1 stabilizes k-MT attachments in prometaphase.
source: For example, Polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1) is an essential mitotic kinase that regulates many aspects of mitosis (extensively reviewed in [Schmucker and Sumara, 2014; Petronczki et al., 2008; van Vugt and Medema, 2005]), including the stabilization of k-MT attachments in prometaphase (Lénárt et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Moutinho-Santos et al., 2012; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Hood et al., 2012; Maia et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to primary literature.

claim: Aurora B kinase destabilizes k-MT attachments to correct k-MT attachment errors.
source: Conversely, Aurora B kinase serves an evolutionarily conserved role for the correction of k-MT attachment errors by destabilizing k-MT attachments (Welburn et al., 2010; Salimian et al., 2011; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Cimini et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to primary literature.

claim: Cdk1 acts in conjunction with either Cyclin A or Cyclin B to drive cell cycle progression into and through mitosis.
source: In addition, Cdk1 acts in conjunction with either Cyclin A or Cyclin B to drive cell cycle progression into and through mitosis (Parry et al., 2003; Vázquez-Novelle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cyclin A2 promotes microtubule dynamics during meiosis II in mouse oocytes to decrease the frequency of merotelic attachments and lagging chromosomes.
source: Similarly, Cyclin A2 has been recently shown to promote microtubule dynamics during meiosis II in mouse oocytes to decrease the frequency of merotelic attachments and the incidence of lagging chromosomes (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent publication.

claim: Prolonged mitotic arrest in taxol for 10 hours is sufficient for selective degradation of Cyclin A without premature mitotic exit.
source: This prolonged mitotic arrest was sufficient for the selective degradation of Cyclin A (den Elzen and Pines, 2001; Geley et al., 2001; Di Fiore and Pines, 2010) without premature mitotic exit as judged by the persistence of substantial levels of Cyclin B and securin (Figure 1B) (Brito and Rieder, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B and citations to previous literature.

claim: The prolonged mitotic arrest strategy did not substantially change the quantities of Plk1, Nek2, or Aurora B kinase.
source: Furthermore, this strategy did not substantially change the quantities of other known mitotic regulators including Plk1, Nek2, or Aurora B kinase, but did show an increase in phospho-Chk2, an indicator of a DNA damage response pathway (Figure 1B) (Matsuoka et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The prolonged mitotic arrest strategy showed an increase in phospho-Chk2, an indicator of a DNA damage response pathway.
source: Furthermore, this strategy did not substantially change the quantities of other known mitotic regulators including Plk1, Nek2, or Aurora B kinase, but did show an increase in phospho-Chk2, an indicator of a DNA damage response pathway (Figure 1B) (Matsuoka et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B and citation to literature on Chk2 phosphorylation.

claim: 41,892 phosphorylation sites on 6288 proteins were identified in four replicate analyses.
source: In four replicate analyses, we identified 41,892 phosphorylation sites on 6288 proteins of which 30,874 phosphorylation sites on 5346 proteins were quantified (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic dataset and summarized in Figure 1C.

claim: 30,874 phosphorylation sites on 5346 proteins were quantified.
source: In four replicate analyses, we identified 41,892 phosphorylation sites on 6288 proteins of which 30,874 phosphorylation sites on 5346 proteins were quantified (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic dataset and summarized in Figure 1C.

claim: 12,609 phosphorylation sites contain the minimal Cdk1 consensus motif (pS/pT-P).
source: 12,609 of these phosphorylation sites contain the minimal Cdk1 consensus motif (pS/pT-P; [Nigg, 1993; Moreno and Nurse, 1990; Songyang et al., 1994]) of which 1264 of these phosphorylation sites with the Cdk1 minimal consensus motif were at least two-fold (average log2 H/L ratio ≥1) more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition compared to the low Cyclin A condition (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citations defining the Cdk1 consensus motif.

claim: 1264 phosphorylation sites with the Cdk1 minimal consensus motif were at least two-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: 12,609 of these phosphorylation sites contain the minimal Cdk1 consensus motif (pS/pT-P; [Nigg, 1993; Moreno and Nurse, 1990; Songyang et al., 1994]) of which 1264 of these phosphorylation sites with the Cdk1 minimal consensus motif were at least two-fold (average log2 H/L ratio ≥1) more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition compared to the low Cyclin A condition (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative phosphoproteomic data.

claim: 135 phosphorylation sites were reproducibly quantified with a p-value of <0.1.
source: Of these phosphorylation sites 135 were reproducibly quantified with a p-value of <0.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: 300 unique phosphorylation sites on 156 proteins with known mitotic roles were identified.
source: Proteins with these phosphorylation sites were additionally filtered for known mitotic roles, which identified 300 (47 with p-value<0.1) unique phosphorylation sites on 156 proteins (30 proteins with p-value<0.1) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the filtered phosphoproteomic dataset.

claim: 118 phosphorylation sites on proteins with known mitotic function contained additional cyclin specificity determinants for an optimal Cdk1 consensus motif (K or R at +2/+3).
source: 118 (22 p-value<0.1) of these phosphorylation sites on proteins with known mitotic function also contained additional cyclin specificity determinants for an optimal Cdk1 consensus motif (K or R at +2/+3) (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1) (Errico et al., 2010; Alexander et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citations defining optimal Cdk1 consensus motifs.

claim: CENP-A has closely spaced Cdk1 consensus motifs at Ser17 and Ser19 that were unchanged between high and low Cyclin A conditions.
source: For example, histone H3-like centromere protein A (CENP-A) has closely spaced Cdk1 consensus motifs at Ser17 and Ser19 that were unchanged between the high and low Cyclin A conditions (Kunitoku et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citation to previous literature on CENP-A phosphorylation.

claim: Lamin B2 has two closely spaced Cdk1 consensus motifs at Thr14 and Ser17 that are sensitive to Cdk1 activity in mitosis but did not significantly change under the experimental conditions.
source: Another example is Lamin B2, a component of the nuclear lamina which has been shown to be phosphorylated by Cyclin B/Cdk1 in vitro and in vivo (Lüscher et al., 1991). Lamin B2 has two closely spaced Cdk1 consensus motifs at Thr14 and Ser17 that are sensitive to Cdk1 activity in mitosis (Petrone et al., 2016), but they did not significantly change under our conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citations to previous literature on Lamin B2 phosphorylation.

claim: Tyrosine residue 15 on Cdk1 was 6-to-8-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: Furthermore, tyrosine residue 15 on Cdk1, was 6-to-8-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr15 inhibits Cdk1 activity.
source: Phosphorylation of Tyr15 inhibits Cdk1 activity (Parker and Piwnica-Worms, 1992), although this negative influence is stronger on Cdk1 (aka cdc2 in those articles) when it is associated with Cyclin B compared to Cyclin A (Clarke et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Cdk1 regulation.

claim: The cells had sufficient Cdk1 activity to enter and maintain mitosis despite Tyr15 phosphorylation.
source: Despite any inhibitory influence of Tyr15 phosphorylation, the cells had sufficient Cdk1 activity to have entered and to maintain mitosis under these experimental conditions (Figure 1B) (Swaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing mitotic markers and citation to literature on Cdk1 activity thresholds.

claim: Haspin kinase phosphorylation at Thr112 was five-fold higher in mitotic cells with high Cyclin A.
source: For example, the level of phosphorylation of protein kinase GSG2 (Haspin kinase) was five-fold higher in mitotic cells with high Cyclin A at the Cdk1 consensus site Thr112, and more than two-fold higher at Cdk1 consensus sites Thr97 and Ser147 (Supplementary file 1) (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citation to literature on Haspin kinase.

claim: Bub1 kinase has adjacent Cdk1 sites at Ser661 and Ser665 with more than two-fold higher phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: Similarly, Bub1 kinase has adjacent Cdk1 sites at Ser661 and Ser665 and the phosphorylation of these sites was more than two-fold higher in our high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1) (Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citation to literature on Bub1 kinase.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Cdk1 site Ser306 on INCENP increased more than four-fold in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: Finally, the phosphorylation of the Cdk1 site Ser306 on Inner Centromere Protein (INCENP) increased more than four-fold in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1) (Honda et al., 2003; Bishop and Schumacher, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citations to literature on INCENP.

claim: Autophosphorylation at Thr232 on Aurora B kinase was more than four-fold higher in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: The functional significance of these specific Cdk1 phosphorylation events remains to be determined, but a net effect of these events could be to increase Aurora B kinase localization and/or activity in prometaphase because the extent of autophosphorylation at Thr232 on Aurora B kinase was more than four-fold higher in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The overall abundance of Aurora B kinase was not affected by changes in levels of Cyclin A during mitosis.
source: The overall abundance of Aurora B kinase was not affected by changes in levels of Cyclin A during mitosis (Figure 1A) indicating that Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity appears to selectively enhance Aurora B kinase activity in mitosis consistent with parallel roles of Cyclin A/Cdk1 and Aurora B kinase in destabilizing k-MT attachments (Welburn et al., 2010; Salimian et al., 2011; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Chan et al., 2012; Cimini et al., 2006; Kabeche and Compton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity appears to selectively enhance Aurora B kinase activity in mitosis.
source: The overall abundance of Aurora B kinase was not affected by changes in levels of Cyclin A during mitosis (Figure 1A) indicating that Cyclin A/Cdk1 activity appears to selectively enhance Aurora B kinase activity in mitosis consistent with parallel roles of Cyclin A/Cdk1 and Aurora B kinase in destabilizing k-MT attachments (Welburn et al., 2010; Salimian et al., 2011; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Chan et al., 2012; Cimini et al., 2006; Kabeche and Compton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the phosphoproteomic data and citations to literature on Aurora B and Cyclin A/Cdk1 functions.

claim: INCENP, Bub1 and Haspin regulate Plk1 localization and activity.
source: With regard to cross-regulation of Plk1, we note extensive evidence that INCENP, Bub1 and Haspin regulate Plk1 localization and activity in addition to their regulatory role on Aurora B kinase (Qi et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2014; Goto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Cdk1 consensus motif containing the dipeptide Ser472:473 on MYPT1 was approximately three-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition (p=0.01).
source: Additionally, the Cdk1 consensus motif containing the dipeptide Ser472:473 on Myosin Phosphatase-Targeting Subunit 1 (MYPT1) was approximately three-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition (p=0.01) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative phosphoproteomic data with statistical significance.

claim: Ser473 on MYPT1 has been shown to be phosphorylated by cdc2 in vitro and to be necessary as a priming phosphorylation for Plk1 interaction.
source: The Ser473 site has previously been shown to be phosphorylated by cdc2 in vitro and to be necessary as a priming phosphorylation for Plk1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (implied by context).

claim: MYPT1 functions to link the catalytic subunit of PP1 to Plk1 to locally dampen Plk1 kinase activity by dephosphorylating the activating Thr210 on Plk1.
source: MYPT1 functions to link the catalytic subunit of PP1 to Plk1 to locally dampen Plk1 kinase activity by dephosphorylating the activating Thr210 (T-loop) on Plk1 (Totsukawa et al., 1999; Yamashiro et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The peptide containing Ser14:Ser18 on PP1-3F was seventeen-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: On PP1-3F, the peptide containing Ser14:Ser18 was seventeen-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition, and on PP1-12C peptides containing Ser399:Ser404, Ser407, Ser509, and Ser604 were each more than two-fold phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Peptides containing Ser399:Ser404, Ser407, Ser509, and Ser604 on PP1-12C were each more than two-fold phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: On PP1-3F, the peptide containing Ser14:Ser18 was seventeen-fold more phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition, and on PP1-12C peptides containing Ser399:Ser404, Ser407, Ser509, and Ser604 were each more than two-fold phosphorylated in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Some Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrates influence the activities of other mitotic regulators during early mitosis.
source: These data indicate that some Cyclin A/Cdk1 substrates influence the activities of other mitotic regulators during early mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the phosphoproteomic data showing changes in Aurora B and Plk1 substrates.

claim: 121 phosphorylation sites on proteins with known mitotic function displayed more than two-fold increase in phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition with Aurora kinase consensus motif.
source: However, we identified 121 (18 p-value<0.1) phosphorylation sites on proteins with known mitotic function that displayed more than two-fold increase in phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data filtered for Aurora kinase consensus motifs.

claim: 94 phosphorylation sites with the Plk1 minimal consensus motif showed greater phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition.
source: However, we identified 94 (20 p-value<0.1) phosphorylation sites with the Plk1 minimal consensus motif that showed greater phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data filtered for Plk1 consensus motifs.

claim: MPS1 displayed more than three-fold higher phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition at a peptide sequence spanning Thr33:Ser37.
source: In addition, dual specificity protein kinase TTK (MPS1) (Jelluma et al., 2008) is in this group of Plk1 substrates that displayed more than three-fold higher phosphorylation in the high Cyclin A condition at a peptide sequence spanning Thr33:Ser37, which contains two sequential Plk1 minimal consensus motifs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citation to literature on MPS1.

claim: The overall abundance of MYPT1 does not change substantially in cells lacking Cyclin A.
source: The overall abundance of MYPT1 does not change substantially in cells lacking Cyclin A, but the level of pMYPT1 Ser473 decreases dramatically (Figure 2C), and there is a significant reduction in pMYPT1 at centromeres of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: The level of pMYPT1 Ser473 decreases dramatically in cells lacking Cyclin A.
source: The overall abundance of MYPT1 does not change substantially in cells lacking Cyclin A, but the level of pMYPT1 Ser473 decreases dramatically (Figure 2C), and there is a significant reduction in pMYPT1 at centromeres of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: There is a significant reduction in pMYPT1 at centromeres of mitotic chromosomes in cells lacking Cyclin A.
source: The overall abundance of MYPT1 does not change substantially in cells lacking Cyclin A, but the level of pMYPT1 Ser473 decreases dramatically (Figure 2C), and there is a significant reduction in pMYPT1 at centromeres of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: There is very little change in the abundance of Cyclin B/Cdk1 in mitotic cells lacking Cyclin A.
source: Importantly, there is very little change in the abundance of Cyclin B/Cdk1 in mitotic cells lacking Cyclin A (Figure 2C) indicating that Ser473 on MYPT1 is sensitive to the levels of Cyclin A/Cdk1 in mitosis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: Ser473 on MYPT1 is sensitive to the levels of Cyclin A/Cdk1 in mitosis.
source: Importantly, there is very little change in the abundance of Cyclin B/Cdk1 in mitotic cells lacking Cyclin A (Figure 2C) indicating that Ser473 on MYPT1 is sensitive to the levels of Cyclin A/Cdk1 in mitosis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from Western blot data showing selective loss of pMYPT1 Ser473 despite maintained Cyclin B levels.

claim: The localization of MYPT1 to kinetochores was disrupted by the absence of Cyclin A.
source: The localization of MYPT1 to kinetochores was also disrupted by the absence of Cyclin A indicating that Cyclin A/Cdk1 phosphorylation is responsible for targeting MYPT1 to kinetochores (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2D.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 phosphorylation is responsible for targeting MYPT1 to kinetochores.
source: The localization of MYPT1 to kinetochores was also disrupted by the absence of Cyclin A indicating that Cyclin A/Cdk1 phosphorylation is responsible for targeting MYPT1 to kinetochores (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from immunofluorescence data showing loss of MYPT1 localization upon Cyclin A depletion.

claim: The overall abundance of Plk1 is not substantially changed in mitotic cells lacking MYPT1.
source: With respect to Plk1 localization and activity, the overall abundance is not substantially changed in mitotic cells lacking either Cyclin A (Figure 1B) or MYPT1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The quantity of Plk1 localized to kinetochores increased in cells depleted of MYPT1.
source: However, quantitative immunofluorescence revealed that the quantity of Plk1 localized to kinetochores increased in cells depleted of MYPT1 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The change in Plk1 abundance at kinetochores was detected in prometaphase but not in metaphase.
source: This change in Plk1 abundance at kinetochores was detected in prometaphase but not in metaphase (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claim: A substantial increase in phosphorylation on Thr210 of Plk1 was detected in mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1.
source: Using a phosphosite-specific Plk1 antibody for Thr210 we detected a substantial increase in phosphorylation on this site in mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in the amount of phosphorylated Plk1 at kinetochores was detected in both prometaphase and metaphase cells lacking MYPT1.
source: Moreover, we detected an increase in the amount of phosphorylated Plk1 at kinetochores in both prometaphase and metaphase cells lacking MYPT1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: MYPT1 recruits the catalytic subunit of PP1 to kinetochores to dephosphorylate the activating loop (Thr210) of Plk1 to dampen Plk1 activity.
source: These data are consistent with previous reports that MYPT1 recruits the catalytic subunit of PP1 to kinetochores to dephosphorylate the activating loop (Thr210) of Plk1 to dampen Plk1 activity (Yamashiro et al., 2008; Totsukawa et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: The stability of k-MT attachments displays a characteristic step-wise increase between prometaphase and metaphase in both RPE1 and U2OS cells.
source: The stability of k-MT attachments display a characteristic step-wise increase between prometaphase and metaphase in both RPE1 and U2OS cells (Figure 4A and Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as we have described previously (Kabeche and Compton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figures 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and citation to previous work.

claim: In prometaphase U2OS cells lacking MYPT1, k-MT attachments were significantly more stable than in control prometaphase cells.
source: In U2OS cells depleted of MYPT1 we observed an inversion of this step-wise change. In prometaphase U2OS cells lacking MYPT1, k-MT attachments were significantly more stable than in control prometaphase cells (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stability of k-MT attachments in RPE1 cells was increased in cells depleted of MYPT1.
source: The stability of k-MT attachments in RPE1 cells was also increased in cells depleted of MYPT1 (Figure 4A), although we only report prometaphase since RPE1 cells display chromosome congression defects in the absence of MYPT1 and are delayed in chromosome alignment and anaphase onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4A.

claim: RPE1 cells display chromosome congression defects in the absence of MYPT1 and are delayed in chromosome alignment and anaphase onset.
source: The stability of k-MT attachments in RPE1 cells was also increased in cells depleted of MYPT1 (Figure 4A), although we only report prometaphase since RPE1 cells display chromosome congression defects in the absence of MYPT1 and are delayed in chromosome alignment and anaphase onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by observation during the experiments.

claim: In metaphase U2OS cells lacking MYPT1, k-MT attachments were significantly less stable than in control metaphase cells.
source: In contrast to the stabilization of k-MT attachments in U2OS cells lacking MYPT1 in prometaphase, k-MT attachments in metaphase cells lacking MYPT1 were significantly less stable than in control metaphase cells (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The k-MT attachments in prometaphase cells lacking MYPT1 were significantly more stable than those of metaphase counterparts.
source: Additionally, the k-MT attachments in prometaphase cells lacking MYPT1 were significantly more stable than those of metaphase counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data comparing prometaphase and metaphase in MYPT1-depleted cells.

claim: Mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1 demonstrated a significant increase in inter-kinetochore distance in both prometaphase and metaphase.
source: In addition to these effects, mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1 demonstrated a significant increase in inter-kinetochore distance in both prometaphase and metaphase and a significant increase in spindle length (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) indicative of a role of MYPT1 in regulating processes that contribute to the mechanical aspects of mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1 demonstrated a significant increase in spindle length.
source: In addition to these effects, mitotic cells depleted of MYPT1 demonstrated a significant increase in inter-kinetochore distance in both prometaphase and metaphase and a significant increase in spindle length (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) indicative of a role of MYPT1 in regulating processes that contribute to the mechanical aspects of mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observed changes in the stability of k-MT attachments in MYPT1-depleted cells were reversed by treatment with low-dose Plk1 inhibitor BI-2536.
source: Importantly, the observed changes in the stability of k-MT attachments were reversed by treatment with low-dose Plk1 inhibitor BI-2536 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data with BI-2536 treatment in Figure 4B.

claim: MYPT1 acts to dampen Plk1 activity at kinetochores during prometaphase to ensure the rapid detachment of k-MTs.
source: This demonstrates that MYPT1 acts to dampen Plk1 activity at kinetochores during prometaphase to ensure the rapid detachment of k-MTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the rescue experiment with Plk1 inhibitor.

claim: Depletion of Cyclin A prematurely stabilized k-MT attachments in prometaphase and eliminated the step-wise increase in k-MT stability between prometaphase and metaphase.
source: As previously reported, depletion of Cyclin A prematurely stabilized k-MT attachments in prometaphase and eliminated the step-wise increase in k-MT stability between prometaphase and metaphase (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C and citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of wild type MYPT1 did not alter the step-wise increase in k-MT stability between prometaphase and metaphase.
source: Expression of wild type MYPT1 did not alter the step-wise increase in k-MT stability between prometaphase and metaphase, although k-MT attachments were slightly less stable in both phases of mitosis in the presence of excess MYPT1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: k-MT attachments were slightly less stable in both phases of mitosis in the presence of excess MYPT1.
source: Expression of wild type MYPT1 did not alter the step-wise increase in k-MT stability between prometaphase and metaphase, although k-MT attachments were slightly less stable in both phases of mitosis in the presence of excess MYPT1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of MYPT1-473A reversed the step-wise change in k-MT attachment stability between prometaphase and metaphase.
source: Expression of MYPT1-473A reversed the step-wise change in k-MT attachment stability between prometaphase and metaphase (Figure 4C) akin to the loss of MYPT1 function (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: Alanine mutation at Ser473 acts in a dominant negative fashion to disrupt endogenous MYPT1 function.
source: This indicates that alanine mutation at this site acts in a dominant negative fashion to disrupt endogenous MYPT1 function.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the MYPT1-473A mutant data.

claim: Expression of either MYPT1-473D or MYPT1-472:473DD abolished the step-wise stabilization of k-MT attachments between prometaphase and metaphase.
source: Expression of either MYPT1-473D or MYPT1-472:473DD abolished the step-wise stabilization of k-MT attachments between prometaphase and metaphase (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells expressing the aspartic acid mutants of MYPT1 displayed k-MT attachment stability equivalent to control cells in prometaphase.
source: Cells expressing the aspartic acid mutants of MYPT1 displayed k-MT attachment stability equivalent to control cells, but did not appropriately stabilize k-MT attachments in metaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: Cells expressing the aspartic acid mutants of MYPT1 did not appropriately stabilize k-MT attachments in metaphase.
source: Cells expressing the aspartic acid mutants of MYPT1 displayed k-MT attachment stability equivalent to control cells, but did not appropriately stabilize k-MT attachments in metaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4C.

claim: The aspartic acid mutants of MYPT1 are acting appropriately during prometaphase (as a phospho-mimic) and remain persistently active in metaphase to inappropriately destabilize k-MT attachments.
source: These data suggest that these mutants of MYPT1 are acting appropriately during prometaphase (as a phospho-mimic) and remain persistently active in metaphase to inappropriately destabilize k-MT attachments.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the photoactivation data with MYPT1 mutants.

claim: The frequency of lagging chromosomes in anaphase was not significantly different between control cells and cells lacking MYPT1 using either U2OS or RPE1 cells.
source: The frequency of lagging chromosomes in anaphase was not significantly different between control cells and cells lacking MYPT1 using either U2OS or RPE1 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of anaphase errors in Figure 4D.

claim: In cells lacking MYPT1, the destabilization of k-MT attachments in metaphase can compensate for the hyperstabilization of k-MT attachments in prometaphase to ensure faithful chromosome segregation.
source: This suggests that in cells lacking MYPT1, the destabilization of k-MT attachments in metaphase can compensate for the hyperstabilization of k-MT attachments in prometaphase to ensure faithful chromosome segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the anaphase error data.

claim: A significant increase in the frequency of lagging chromosomes in anaphase was observed in cells lacking MYPT1 following release from monastrol-induced mitotic arrest.
source: However, if we increased the frequency of k-MT attachment errors using the Eg5 inhibitor monastrol, then we observed a significant increase in the frequency of lagging chromosomes in anaphase in cells lacking MYPT1 relative to control cells following the release from the monastrol-induced mitotic arrest (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of anaphase errors after monastrol washout in Figure 4E.

claim: MYPT1-deficient cells are compromised in correcting k-MT attachment errors under conditions where the frequency of errors is elevated.
source: Thus, MYPT1-deficient cells are compromised in correcting k-MT attachment errors under conditions where the frequency of errors is elevated.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the monastrol washout experiment.

claim: The association of Plk1 with substrates is dependent on priming phosphorylation on the substrate, which is frequently carried out by Cdk1.
source: The association of Plk1 with substrates is dependent on priming phosphorylation on the substrate, which is frequently carried out by Cdk1 (Lee et al., 2014; Schmucker and Sumara, 2014; Kang et al., 2006; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Elia et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The association of MYPT1 with Plk1 was previously shown to be mediated by priming phosphorylation at Ser473.
source: The association of MYPT1 with Plk1 was previously shown to be mediated by priming phosphorylation at Ser473 (Yamashiro et al., 2008), and our data indicate that Cyclin A/Cdk1 catalyzes that priming phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Plk1 localization to kinetochores is regulated by self-priming phosphorylation of PBIP1 (CENP-U) by Plk1 itself.
source: While Plk1 substrate recognition depends on priming phosphorylation commonly by Cdk1, Plk1 localization to kinetochores is regulated by self-priming phosphorylation of PBIP1 (CENP-U) by Plk1 itself (Kang et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of Plk1 activity results in its delocalization from kinetochores.
source: Indeed, inhibition of Plk1 activity results in its delocalization from kinetochores (Kang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cells depleted of either Cyclin A or MYPT1 displayed an approximate two-fold increase in the level of phosphorylation at Thr78 on PBIP1 as judged by immunoblotting of mitotic extracts.
source: Cells depleted of either Cyclin A or MYPT1 displayed an approximate two-fold increase in the level of phosphorylation at Thr78 compared to control cells as judged by immunoblotting of mitotic extracts (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: There was a significant increase in the localization of pPBIP1 Thr78 to kinetochores in cells lacking either Cyclin A or MYPT1.
source: There was also a significant increase in the localization of pPBIP1 Thr78 to kinetochores in cells lacking either Cyclin A or MYPT1 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 promotes MYPT1 targeting to kinetochores where it reduces the level of Plk1 phosphorylation at Thr210 and reduces the level of Plk1 self-priming of PBIP1.
source: These data indicate that Cyclin A/Cdk1 promotes MYPT1 targeting to kinetochores where it reduces the level of Plk1 phosphorylation at Thr210 and reduces the level of Plk1 self-priming of PBIP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the combined data on MYPT1, Plk1, and PBIP1.

claim: The identity of the specific activating cyclin subunit can confer selectivity onto Cdk1 for some substrates in mammalian cells.
source: These data provide evidence in mammalian cells that the identity of the specific activating cyclin subunit can confer selectivity onto Cdk1 for some substrates (Pagliuca et al., 2011; Loog and Morgan, 2005; Errico et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2003; Brown et al., 1999; Bhaduri and Pryciak, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Many mitotic substrates are likely to be phosphorylated with equivalent efficiency by Cyclin A/Cdk1 or Cyclin B/Cdk1.
source: Whereas many mitotic substrates are likely to be phosphorylated with equivalent efficiency by Cyclin A/Cdk1 or Cyclin B/Cdk1 as indicated by enzyme-substrate interaction data and cyclin-substitution rescue experiments in yeast and HeLa cells (Pagliuca et al., 2011; Swaffer et al., 2016; Fisher and Nurse, 1996; Gong and Ferrell, 2010; Gavet and Pines, 2010), we show that the phosphorylation of a subset of Cdk1 substrates in mammalian cells relies on the continued presence of Cyclin A in prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The phosphorylation of a subset of Cdk1 substrates in mammalian cells relies on the continued presence of Cyclin A in prometaphase.
source: Whereas many mitotic substrates are likely to be phosphorylated with equivalent efficiency by Cyclin A/Cdk1 or Cyclin B/Cdk1 as indicated by enzyme-substrate interaction data and cyclin-substitution rescue experiments in yeast and HeLa cells (Pagliuca et al., 2011; Swaffer et al., 2016; Fisher and Nurse, 1996; Gong and Ferrell, 2010; Gavet and Pines, 2010), we show that the phosphorylation of a subset of Cdk1 substrates in mammalian cells relies on the continued presence of Cyclin A in prometaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing selective loss of phosphorylation in Cyclin A-depleted cells.

claim: Ongoing phosphatase activity diminishes the level of phosphorylation of Cyclin A-sensitive substrates in Cyclin A-deficient mitotic cells, despite the continued presence of Cyclin B/Cdk1.
source: Ongoing phosphatase activity diminishes the level of phosphorylation of these substrates in Cyclin A-deficient mitotic cells, despite the continued presence of Cyclin B/Cdk1 (Figures 1B and 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from Western blot data showing loss of phosphorylation despite maintained Cyclin B levels.

claim: Three subsets of mitotic Cdk1 substrates exist in mammalian cells defined by whether they are selectively phosphorylated by Cyclin A/Cdk1, Cyclin B/Cdk1, or non-selectively phosphorylated by either.
source: Thus, we envisage three subsets of mitotic Cdk1 substrates in mammalian cells that are defined by whether they are selectively phosphorylated by Cyclin A/Cdk1, Cyclin B/Cdk1, or non-selectively phosphorylated by either Cyclin A/Cdk1 or Cyclin B/Cdk1; these substrates would display temporal differences in phosphorylation because Cyclin A and Cyclin B are degraded asynchronously during mitosis in mammalian cells (den Elzen and Pines, 2001; Geley et al., 2001; Di Fiore and Pines, 2010; Brito and Rieder, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and citations to literature on cyclin degradation timing.

claim: The priming of MYPT1 for Plk1 interaction is sensitive to Cyclin A/Cdk1.
source: Our finding that the priming of MYPT1 for Plk1 interaction is sensitive to Cyclin A/Cdk1 reveals a new, and unexpected level of temporal control in the process of Plk1 substrate priming.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing Cyclin A-dependent phosphorylation of MYPT1.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1-catalyzed priming of MYPT1 provides an inherent bias favoring the interaction of MYPT1 and Plk1 during early mitosis.
source: Cyclin A/Cdk1-catalyzed priming of MYPT1 provides an inherent bias favoring the interaction of MYPT1 and Plk1 during early mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the temporal pattern of Cyclin A expression and MYPT1 phosphorylation.

claim: MYPT1 priming would be expected to diminish once Cyclin A is degraded as cells reach metaphase.
source: This priming would be expected to diminish once Cyclin A is degraded as cells reach metaphase, which fits a need in prometaphase to titrate the k-MT stabilizing effect of Plk1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the known timing of Cyclin A degradation and the observed effects on k-MT stability.

claim: Self-priming and Cdk1-dependent priming of Plk1 substrates were previously considered as independent, unrelated processes.
source: Self-priming and Cdk1-dependent priming of Plk1 substrates were previously considered as independent, unrelated processes (Lee et al., 2014; Schmucker and Sumara, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The autonomous, feed-forward mechanism of self-priming of Plk1 substrates can be constrained by the Cdk1-dependent priming of substrates.
source: This finding implies that the autonomous, feed-forward mechanism of self-priming of Plk1 substrates can be constrained by the Cdk1-dependent priming of substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data showing MYPT1 regulation of PBIP1 phosphorylation.

claim: This constraint on Plk1 self-priming is important to prevent excessive activation of Plk1 which could hyper-stabilize k-MT attachments and impair the efficient correction of k-MT attachment errors.
source: With respect to pools of Plk1 acting at kinetochores (Lera et al., 2016), this constraint is important to prevent excessive activation of Plk1 which could hyper-stabilize k-MT attachments and impair the efficient correction of k-MT attachment errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the functional data and citation to literature on Plk1 localization.

claim: Cyclin A/Cdk1 can destabilize k-MT attachments by directly phosphorylating substrates or indirectly by influencing the activities of other mitotic kinases.
source: Cyclin A/Cdk1 promotes the destabilization of k-MT attachments in prometaphase (Kabeche and Compton, 2013; Zhang et al., 2017), and it can do so by directly phosphorylating substrates or indirectly by influencing the activities of other mitotic kinases.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: In the presence of Cyclin A, there is increased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Aurora B kinase.
source: In the presence of Cyclin A, we observe increased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Aurora B kinase which plays a well characterized role in destabilizing k-MT attachments to promote error correction (Welburn et al., 2010; Salimian et al., 2011; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Cimini et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012), and decreased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Plk1 which plays a role in stabilizing k-MT attachments in early mitosis (Lénárt et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Moutinho-Santos et al., 2012; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010; Hood et al., 2012; Maia et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomic data and citations to literature on Aurora B function.

claim: In the presence of Cyclin A, there is decreased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Plk1.
source: In the presence of Cyclin A, we observe increased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Aurora B kinase which plays a well characterized role in destabilizing k-MT attachments to promote error correction (Welburn et al., 2010; Salimian et al., 2011; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson and Cheeseman, 2011; Cimini et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012), and decreased phosphorylation of the activating T-loop on Plk1 which plays a role in stabilizing k-MT attachments in early mitosis (Lénárt et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Moutinho-Santos et al., 2012; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010; Hood et al., 2012; Maia et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data showing increased pPlk1 in the absence of Cyclin A or MYPT1.

claim: k-MT attachment stability at each phase of mitosis is a readout of integrated, opposing inputs from multiple kinases and phosphatases.
source: These data underscore the importance of systems-based views of mitotic signaling networks in that k-MT attachment stability at each phase of mitosis is a readout of integrated, opposing inputs from multiple kinases and phosphatases.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the comprehensive data showing interconnected regulation.
